passage: I'm Leela, Harsha's cousin, and I stayed at their house during the holidays. Before dinner, Harsha dragged his little stool to the sink on his own, rubbed the soap into bubbles and held his wet hands up for the towel, grinning. But at bedtime, when his mother brought his pyjamas, he threw himself on the floor, kicking and yelling "No!" I couldn't tell if he was tired or just wanted to keep playing. Maybe both.

qa.q: What did Harsha drag to the sink before dinner?
qa.a: He dragged his little stool to the sink on his own.

qa.q: How can you tell Harsha felt proud of washing his hands?
qa.a: He held his wet hands up for the towel, grinning, which suggests he liked doing the routine himself.

qa.q: What could help Harsha's bedtime go more smoothly?
qa.a: His mother could give a gentle warning before bedtime and let him choose between two pyjamas, keeping the same calm steps each night.

qa.q: Why might Leela be unsure about the reason for Harsha's tantrum?
qa.a: Leela only sees what he does from the outside, so Leela can guess tiredness or wanting to play but can't know which it was.

grounding: Shows a toddler following a handwashing routine but resisting bedtime with a tantrum, seen by a cousin.

passage:
Tuesday: When Nirmala started the tidy-up song, Ojas flung a block across the room and lay face down on the rug, howling.
Friday: She sang again and dropped one car into the basket. Ojas watched, then put in two cars himself before wandering off.
The next Thursday: Hearing the first line of the song, Ojas began carrying blocks to the basket, humming along, and looked up at Nirmala after each one.

qa.q: What did Nirmala do on Friday while singing?
qa.a: She sang again and dropped one car into the basket.

qa.q: What does Ojas looking up at Nirmala after each block suggest he wanted?
qa.a: It suggests he wanted her to notice and share his pleasure in helping tidy up.

qa.q: Why did the tidy-up song help Ojas learn the routine?
qa.a: The same song each time signalled what was coming, and Nirmala tidying with him made it feel like a shared game rather than an order. 🎉

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt on the first Tuesday?
qa.a: She may have felt tired or frustrated by the howling, yet she kept the song going on later days.

grounding: Shows a toddler moving from resisting a toy-pickup routine with a tantrum to joining it over time.

passage: It was brushing time in their small Pune flat. Uma, two and a half, clamped her mouth shut and turned her face into the pillow when Alka held out the toothbrush. Alka didn't argue. She handed Uma her cloth doll and a second brush. "Can you brush Guddi's teeth?" Uma scrubbed the doll's face hard, giggling. Then she opened her own mouth wide, and Alka brushed quickly while Uma watched Guddi.

qa.q: What did Alka hand Uma along with the second brush?
qa.a: She handed Uma her cloth doll.

qa.q: Why might Uma have clamped her mouth shut at first?
qa.a: She may have felt tired or wanted some control over her own body, so she resisted the routine.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Alka, and why?
qa.a: Letting Uma brush the doll first turned the routine into play and gave her some control, so she opened her mouth willingly.

qa.q: What would change if Alka had forced the brush into Uma's mouth?
qa.a: Brushing might become a nightly fight, and Uma could start dreading bedtime.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler resisting a bedtime routine and then joining it through play.

passage:
"Yamini, bath time's over. Teeth now."
"No teeth!" Yamini flung the brush on the floor and flopped down.
"Hmm." Harsha sat beside her. "Who brushes first, you or Teddy?"
She peeked. "Teddy."
Harsha brushed the bear's fuzzy mouth. "Your turn."
"Me do!" She grabbed the brush and chewed it, grinning.
"Good job. Then story, then sleep."
"Two story!"
"One story, Yamini."

qa.q: Who brushed first before Yamini?
qa.a: Teddy, her bear, got brushed first.

qa.q: Why did Yamini fling the brush and flop down?
qa.a: She did not want to stop playing and resisted the routine, feeling frustrated at being told what to do.

qa.q: Which choice by Harsha worked, and why?
qa.a: Turning brushing into a game with Teddy let Yamini feel in charge, so she joined in instead of fighting.

qa.q: What would change if Harsha had shouted and forced the brush in?
qa.a: Bedtime might have become a battle, and Yamini could start dreading the routine instead of slowly accepting it.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler moving between resisting and accepting a bedtime hygiene routine.

passage:
Weekly crèche note, by Ganga Didi
Omkar is learning 'tidy-up time'. On Monday he threw himself down and kicked when the bell rang. On Wednesday he put two cars in the basket after I sang our clean-up song. Today he carried the whole basket to the shelf himself and looked at me, chest out. 🙂 He still cries when it's time to wash hands, so we are working on that next.

qa.q: What did Omkar do on Monday when the bell rang?
qa.a: He threw himself down and kicked.

qa.q: What does Omkar looking at Ganga Didi with his chest out suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt proud of carrying the basket and wanted her to notice.

qa.q: How could Ganga Didi use what worked for tidy-up with handwashing?
qa.a: She could add a short song or a fun step to handwashing too, since the song helped tidy-up become a routine.

qa.q: How might Omkar's parents feel reading this note?
qa.a: They may feel encouraged by his progress and understanding about the handwashing crying, since it shows he is still learning.

grounding: Shows a toddler slowly adopting a toy-pickup routine while still resisting handwashing.

passage: Before every meal in their village house, Manjula took her granddaughter Mahima to the brass lota by the back step. Today Mahima, two, wanted her roti now. She stamped, shouted "No wash!" and sat down in the dust. Manjula poured a little water over her own hands and sang the soap song. Mahima watched, then held out her fists, rubbed them together, and splashed so much that both of them laughed.

qa.q: Where does Manjula take Mahima before every meal?
qa.a: To the brass lota by the back step.

qa.q: Why did Mahima stamp and shout "No wash!"?
qa.a: She was hungry and impatient, and the washing felt like it was keeping her from her roti.

qa.q: What worked in getting Mahima to wash, and why?
qa.a: Manjula washing her own hands and singing turned it into a game Mahima wanted to copy.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel about this daily routine?
qa.a: Patient, and quietly pleased that the habit is sticking even with some stamping.

grounding: Shows a toddler resisting and then joining a handwashing routine before meals.

passage: In their flat in Nairobi, Wanjiru sang the tidy-up song and held open the toy basket. Her son Hiroshi, two and a half, threw one wooden car in, then lay flat on his back and kicked. "No tidy!" She sat down beside him and dropped a car in herself, making a crash sound. He sat up. She did it again. By the fourth car he was racing her, and when the rug was clear he pushed the basket to its corner himself.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi throw in first?
qa.a: One wooden car.

qa.q: What does Hiroshi lying on his back and kicking suggest?
qa.a: He was frustrated and unwilling to stop playing just to tidy up.

qa.q: Which choice by Wanjiru turned it around, and why?
qa.a: Joining in with crash sounds made tidying a game, so he wanted to take part.

qa.q: What would change if Wanjiru had tidied everything herself?
qa.a: The rug would be clear faster, but Hiroshi would miss the chance to build the habit.

grounding: Shows a toddler resisting and then taking part in tidying up toys.

passage: I'm Damini, Sudha's older sister. In the summer holidays it stays light till late, and bedtime has turned into a fight. Last night Sudha, who is two, ran round the bed shouting "Not sleepy!" while Amma held her pyjamas. Then Amma drew the curtains, switched on the small lamp and started the same story as always. Sudha stopped, climbed under the sheet and held out her foot for the pyjamas. I think she likes knowing what comes next.

qa.q: What did Sudha shout while running round the bed?
qa.a: She shouted "Not sleepy!"

qa.q: What might Sudha have been feeling when she ran round the bed?
qa.a: She was probably excited and restless, since it was still light and bedtime felt too early.

qa.q: What helped Sudha settle, and how could the family keep it up?
qa.a: The familiar steps of curtains, small lamp and the same story; keeping that order every night helps.

qa.q: How does Damini explain Sudha's change?
qa.a: She thinks Sudha likes knowing what comes next, so the routine calms her.

grounding: Shows a toddler resisting bedtime in summer and settling once a familiar routine begins.

passage:
First day of the summer holidays. Leela, Ira's mother, says, "Wash hands before mango." Ira, two, screams and hides under the table.
Three days later. Leela sings a tap song and lets Ira squeeze the soap herself. Ira giggles, rubs bubbles on her nose, and eats her mango.
Two weeks later. When the mango plate comes out, Ira runs to the basin before anyone speaks, singing the song wrong but loud.

qa.q: Where does Ira run when the mango plate comes out?
qa.a: To the basin.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling on the first day when she hid under the table?
qa.a: Ira felt resistant and upset, not wanting to stop for handwashing.

qa.q: What helped Ira accept the routine?
qa.a: Turning it into a song and letting her squeeze the soap herself made it fun and gave her some control.

qa.q: How might Leela feel when Ira runs to the basin unprompted?
qa.a: Leela would likely feel pleased and amused, glad the routine has become Ira's own.

grounding: Over the summer mango season, a toddler moves from resisting handwashing to doing it on her own.

passage: The week before Eid, everyone in Nazia's Hyderabad flat was cleaning. Kavitha Aunty, who helped at home, sang, "Toys in the basket, one, two, three!" Nazia, two, threw a block across the room instead and laughed. Kavitha didn't scold. She put one block in and waited. Nazia watched, picked up a doll, and dropped it in. "Three!" Kavitha cheered. Nazia raced around grabbing toys until the basket overflowed.

qa.q: What did Kavitha Aunty sing?
qa.a: Toys in the basket, one, two, three!

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she threw a block and laughed?
qa.a: Nazia felt playful and excited, testing the rule rather than following it.

qa.q: How did Kavitha turn resistance into cooperation?
qa.a: She didn't scold; she modelled putting one block in, waited, and cheered Nazia's first try.

qa.q: How might Nazia's family feel seeing the full basket?
qa.a: They would probably feel pleased and amused that tidying became a game.

grounding: During pre-Eid cleaning, a toddler shifts from throwing toys to tidying them with a playful helper.

passage:
"Bath, brush, bed," Nilesh told his son. The Ganpati drums were still going down the lane.
"No bed! Dum dum!" Ojas, two, ran in circles.
"Drums tomorrow too. First bath."
"No bath!"
"Okay, you choose. Duck or boat in the bath?"
Ojas stopped. "Boat."
"Boat it is."
After the bath, Nilesh held out the toothbrush. "Who brushes, you or me?"
"Me!"
"Then bed. Story or song?"
"Song. Bappa song."
Nilesh sang softly. Ojas's eyes closed before the second verse.

qa.q: Which toy did Ojas choose for the bath?
qa.a: Boat.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling when he ran in circles shouting 'No bed!'?
qa.a: Ojas felt excited and resistant, stirred up by the festival drums.

qa.q: How did Nilesh get Ojas through the routine without a tantrum?
qa.a: He kept the same steps but offered small choices, duck or boat, who brushes, story or song, so Ojas felt in control.

qa.q: How might Nilesh feel when Ojas falls asleep before the second verse?
qa.a: Nilesh probably feels relieved and tender, glad the routine worked on a noisy festival night.

grounding: On a noisy Ganpati festival night, a father keeps a toddler's bedtime routine using small choices.

passage:
Crèche note, summer.

Payal, two, used to cry every time we washed hands before lunch. The water was "cold" and she pulled her hands away.

This week we started the handwashing song: rub-rub, clap-clap, splash. Today she went to the basin on her own, stood on the step, and sang it while rubbing her hands. She shook them dry and said, "Done!" 😊 — Urmila

qa.q: What did Payal say after shaking her hands dry?
qa.a: She said, "Done!"

qa.q: How did Payal feel about handwashing before the song?
qa.a: Payal was upset and resistant, crying and pulling her hands away.

qa.q: What helped Payal accept the handwashing routine?
qa.a: The handwashing song made it fun and gave her simple steps to follow.

qa.q: How might Urmila feel seeing Payal wash her hands on her own?
qa.a: Urmila was likely pleased and proud of her progress.

grounding: A crèche note records a toddler moving from resisting handwashing to doing it willingly with a song.

passage:
It was the rainy season in the village near Dharwad, and Aditi, two, had spent the afternoon indoors scattering her wooden animals across the floor.

Shankar Ajja held up the basket. "Time to put them to sleep."

Aditi threw herself on the floor and wailed. "No!"

Ajja sat beside her. "The cow first." She sniffed, picked up the cow, and dropped it in the basket. Then the goat. Then all the rest.

qa.q: What did Ajja hold up?
qa.a: He held up the basket.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling when she threw herself on the floor?
qa.a: Aditi was frustrated and upset, not wanting playtime to end.

qa.q: How did Shankar Ajja help Aditi with the toy-pickup routine?
qa.a: He stayed calm, made it a game of putting the animals to sleep, and started with just one.

qa.q: How might Ajja feel during Aditi's tantrum?
qa.a: Ajja seemed patient and gentle, perhaps amused, choosing to help rather than scold.

grounding: During the rainy season, a toddler resists a toy-pickup routine and then follows it with her grandfather's patient help.

passage:
During Lunar New Year in Singapore, the fireworks had kept everyone up late for three nights. Mei, two, refused to brush her teeth.

"No brush!" she shouted, hiding behind the sofa.

Kwame, her father, knelt down. "Your dinosaur needs his teeth brushed first." He brushed the toy's teeth, then held out the brush.

Mei came out slowly. She let him brush her teeth, then climbed into bed.

qa.q: Where did Mei hide?
qa.a: She hid behind the sofa.

qa.q: How was Mei feeling when she shouted "No brush"?
qa.a: Mei was tired and cranky, upset after late nights and a broken routine.

qa.q: How did Kwame help Mei get back to her bedtime routine?
qa.a: He made it playful by brushing the dinosaur's teeth first, which helped her join in.

qa.q: How might Kwame feel after the festival nights?
qa.a: Kwame was probably tired too, but patient with Mei.

grounding: During Lunar New Year, a toddler resists her bedtime routine after late nights, and her father helps her return to it.

passage: I'm Gurpreet, staying with Hafsa's family this week. At seven every evening her Ammi sings the tidy-up song. On Monday, Hafsa threw the blocks, lay on the floor and kicked. By Thursday she dropped three blocks in the basket, then washed her hands at the low sink, splashing happily. Tonight she yawned, fetched her own toothbrush and held it up. Her brother Imran said, "She's faster than me now!" and raced her to the bathroom.

qa.q: What did Hafsa fetch tonight?
qa.a: She fetched her own toothbrush and held it up.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's kicking on Monday suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt upset and frustrated at having to stop playing when the tidy-up song began.

qa.q: What helped Hafsa settle into the routine, and what could keep it going?
qa.a: The same song at the same time every evening made it predictable; keeping that and letting her do small parts herself would help.

qa.q: How does Imran see Hafsa's new habits?
qa.a: Imran finds it fun and a little competitive, racing her to the bathroom now that she's quick.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler moving from tantrums at tidy-up time to following an evening routine.
